sampling: Native -O2 servers receive 1, 16 or 256 calls over one reused connection, three fresh server processes per case. Counters begin after listener/routing/root setup. Per-call samples follow serving-task removal; final samples require client disconnect and no serving/I/O/other tasks while the listener remains open. A measurement-only wake of the existing listener allows retirement of the final finished task without adding a task or connection.
limits: Tracing is disabled and physical freeing enabled. Native clients check matching outputs against interpreted and ordinary native servers. Managed storage and cumulative allocation categories do not identify individual live objects. Raw request/wire buffers, stack pools, TLS/OS/allocator metadata, whole-process memory and timing are excluded. Lower retained storage does not establish complete server ownership, checked ARC, lower execution time, zero-cost abstractions or C/Rust parity.

Inlined helpers may lack standalone symbols; inspect instructions, ownership operations and register/stack use. No timing or zero-overhead claim follows from symbols.

observations: g_apply_user at 0x33340 reserves 488 bytes plus 48 saved-register bytes (536 total, excluding incoming return address), 16 fewer than storage candidate e6455c0d. It spills method id and argument pointer at rsp+0xc/+0x10 across setjmp. At 0x334b1..0x334cc it loads the function table, indexes its 32-byte entries, loads owning metadata at offset 24, and calls the typed entry directly. This helper has no method-closure allocation or generic application call.

g_run_method at 0x31b40 uses a 536-byte fixed frame plus aligned argument storage, 32 fixed bytes more than e6455c0d. Measured one-parameter methods use 32 dynamic bytes. At 0x31bea..0x31c10 it sizes/zeros the slots; r14 holds their address and it spills to rbp-0xf0. Typed value cleanup is registered at 0x31c87..0x31cb8 and method dispatch is at 0x32360.

g_method_values_release at 0x32fc0 uses 24 saved-register bytes. It clears the pending count before typed argument disposal at 0x32fe8, clears result/error words with movups at 0x32ff5, and invokes their concrete destruction functions. It allocates no owner record.

The output cursor is inlined into g_run_method. It reads runtime allocation metadata to distinguish shared nodes; the unique path clears the continuation field at 0x325d6 and calls fwp_apply_owned at 0x325e6. Shared nodes use fwp_apply_borrowed_prefix at 0x325fa. These ownership checks still cost instructions; the change does not establish zero-cost iteration.

g_apply_user, g_run_method, g_method_values_release and g_job_peer_finish have exactly the same instructions as the reviewed unary-strings binary. Incoming iterator construction still uses generic owned application at 0x320d1.

The four reviewed helpers exactly match the unary-strings binary. Output-channel construction still allocates separate channel/context records and sends still mark values for tracing; the subsequent channel preparation addresses that boundary.

hosts.scope:
# Measuring memory in a server after repeated calls

A remote call runs part of a program in another process. Earlier client
measurements exclude that server process; they cannot prove its values or
serving tasks are released. This baseline measures the native server itself.

Each client takes a call count on the command line. `I64` is a signed 64-bit
integer. `consume : I64 -> I64` takes a call index and returns its numeric result;
the channel variant adds `! {Async}` to declare task/channel operations.
`const` supplies the same input for each call; `step` adds the response to an accumulated total. `curry`
adapts the tuple-taking body of `step` to the two arguments supplied by fold.
The four workloads are:

- `unary-strings`: send a 64-character name and receive a greeting. The server
  adds the seven characters `hello, `, so each result has length 71.
- `response-stream`: ask for integers 1 through 64 and sum them, giving 2,080.
  An iterator produces these values as the caller requests them.
- `request-stream`: send those 64 integers and receive their sum, 2,080.
- `channel-output`: ask the server to send `tick 1` through `tick 64` into a
  channel, a queue used to communicate between tasks. Close and drain the queue
  after the call, then add the string lengths, giving 439.

Each measured server process receives 1, 16 or 256 sequential calls from one
client, with three fresh server processes per case. The client uses ordinary
connection reuse. Samples follow serving-task removal from the scheduler;
physical task-record freeing is measured separately by the resulting managed
storage. The final sample waits for client disconnection and removal of all
connection and serving tasks. The server remains alive with its listener open.

Generated clients and servers use native `-O2`. Collection is disabled and
physical freeing enabled. Counters begin after
listener, routing and root-task setup. They cover managed allocation requests,
requested/charged bytes, reference-count increments and selected allocation
categories. Categories count allocations, not identities of remaining objects.
Raw request/wire buffers, stack pools, TLS/OS/allocator metadata, whole-process
memory and timing are excluded. Both an interpreted server and ordinary native
server provide functional output references. No timing or C/Rust comparison is
claimed; the baseline does not establish server ownership or checked ARC.

An idle scheduler can remain on the last finished task's stack until another
task becomes ready. The measurement wakes the existing listener once, after
the connection closes and all spawned tasks finish, so the ordinary scheduler
can retire that final task before sampling. This adds no task or connection;
comparisons must use the same wake and drain boundary.
